verses.translation: And the seventh{H7637} messenger{H4397} blasts{H8628}, and there were many{H7235} voices{H6963} in the heavens{H8064}, saying: The rich{H6223} of this world{H5769} go{H1980}, all of them, after our lord{H113} Yeshua{H3442}, and he shall rule{H4910} from everlasting{H5769} and unto everlasting{H5769}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם ('from everlasting unto everlasting') — the exact psalm formula from Psalm 90:2, 103:17, 1 Chronicles 16:36. Greek has εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('unto the ages of ages'). A back-translator from Greek would write לעולמי עולמים ('to ages of ages'), not the psalm formula.

Uses יִמְשֹׁל (yimshol — 'shall rule/have dominion', H4910) — the governance verb from Genesis 1:16-18, 3:16, 37:8. Greek βασιλεύσει means specifically 'shall reign as king.' A back-translator from Greek would use יִמְלוֹךְ (yimloch — 'shall reign,' from מלך H4427), the exact cognate of βασιλεύω. The Hebrew ימשל implies dominion; the Greek βασιλεύω implies royal enthronement.

Uses תֹּקֵעַ (toqea — 'blasts,' H8628) — the specific verb for shofar blowing in the Torah's warfare and festival contexts (Num 10:3-10, Josh 6:4-20, Judg 3:27, 7:18-22). A natural Hebrew author reaches for this deeply rooted OT term.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the rich (עשירים) of this world go, all of them, after our lord Yeshua.' Greek: 'the kingdoms (βασιλεῖαι) of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord and of his Christ' (τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν καὶ τοῦ χριστοῦ αὐτοῦ). Completely different — individual wealthy people following vs. political entities transferring sovereignty.
Hebrew names ישוע (Yeshua) explicitly as a single figure. Greek says 'our Lord AND his Christ' (κυρίου ἡμῶν καὶ τοῦ χριστοῦ αὐτοῦ) — two distinct referents.
Hebrew: 'from everlasting to everlasting' (psalm formula). Greek: 'unto the ages of ages' (Hellenistic formula).
translation_notes: The consonantal עשירים (with shin) can only be 'rich ones' (H6223). There is no consonantal ambiguity. The Hebrew text genuinely presents a different scene from the Greek — the wealthy submitting, rather than kingdoms transferring.
textual_notes: Psalm 90:2 — מֵעוֹלָם עַד עוֹלָם אַתָּה אֵל ('from everlasting to everlasting, you are God'). The Hebrew formula attributes to the anointed one a phrase reserved for YHWH in the Psalms.

verses.translation: And twenty{H6242}-four{H702} elders{H2205} sitting{H3427} upon their thrones{H3678} before{H6440} YHWH{H3068} fall{H5307} upon their faces{H6440} and pray{H6419} to YHWH{H3068}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מִתְפַּלְּלִים (mitpallelim — 'praying,' H6419, hitpael reflexive of פלל) — the distinctly Hebrew prayer verb, carrying connotations of intercession and self-judgment (Gen 20:7, 1 Sam 1:10,12,26-27, 1 Kings 8:28-54, Dan 9:4). Greek has προσεκύνησαν ('worshipped/prostrated'). A back-translator from Greek would use מִשְׁתַּחֲוִים (mishtachavim — 'bowing/worshipping'), not the prayer verb. The Hebrew says they PRAY; the Greek says they WORSHIP.
Uses יַהְוֶה (YHWH, H3068) twice. Greek has τῷ θεῷ ('God'). A back-translator from Greek would use אֱלֹהִים (Elohim), not the personal Name.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'pray to YHWH' (מתפללים ליהוה). Greek: 'worshipped God' (προσεκύνησαν τῷ θεῷ). Different verb and different divine designation.
Hebrew: 'before YHWH' (לפני יהוה). Greek: 'before God' (ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ). Same pattern throughout this chapter — Hebrew consistently uses the personal Name.
translation_notes: The hitpael form מתפללים implies reflexive engagement — they 'pray themselves' before YHWH, not merely perform an external act of worship.

verses.translation: And saying: We give{H5414} praise{H7623} to you, Lord{H113} of Hosts{H6635}, the one who was{H1961} and is{H1933} and shall be{H1961}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses אֲדוֹן צְבָאוֹת ('Lord of Hosts,' H113+H6635) — a variant of the standard OT divine title (cf. Isa 1:24, 3:1, 10:16,33, 19:4). Greek has κύριε ὁ θεὸς ὁ παντοκράτωρ ('Lord God Almighty'). A back-translator from Greek 'Almighty' (παντοκράτωρ) would use שַׁדַּי (Shaddai) or כָּל־יָכוֹל ('all-powerful'), NOT צבאות ('Hosts/armies').

CRITICAL: The tripartite formula הֶהָיָה וְהֹוֶה וְיִהְיֶה ('the one who was, and is, and shall be') derives ALL THREE tenses from the root היה/הוה — the very root from which the divine Name YHWH is understood to derive (Ex 3:14). This name-play is ONLY possible in Hebrew. Greek has ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν ('the one who is and who was') — using unrelated Greek verbs with no connection to a divine Name. The Hebrew author is UNPACKING the Tetragrammaton. A Greek author could never produce this play on the Hebrew divine Name.

Hebrew: 'we give praise' (נותנים שבח). Greek: εὐχαριστοῦμέν σοι ('we give thanks to you'). Different — praise (שבח) vs. thanks (εὐχαριστέω). A back-translator from Greek would use מוֹדִים (modim — 'we give thanks'), not שבח.
greek_deviations: Greek 11:17 continues: ὅτι εἴληφας τὴν δύναμίν σου τὴν μεγάλην καὶ ἐβασίλευσας ('because you have taken your great power and have reigned'). This entire clause is ABSENT from the Hebrew.

Many Greek TR manuscripts omit 'and who is to come' (καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος) in 11:17. The Hebrew preserves all three temporal aspects (was, is, shall be). Where Greek does include the third aspect, it uses ἐρχόμενος ('coming') — a DIFFERENT concept from 'shall be' (יהיה).
translation_notes: וְהֹוֶה (vehove) — the present participle of the archaic root הוה (H1933), meaning 'existing/being.' This root is virtually absent from standard biblical prose but appears in Ecclesiastes (2:22, 11:3) and is the backbone of the Tetragrammaton.
textual_notes: Exodus 3:14 — אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה ('I will be what I will be'). The tripartite formula in this verse expands this same root across all three temporal dimensions — past (הָיָה), present (הֹוֶה), and future (יִהְיֶה).

verses.translation: And the peoples{H5971} were filled{H4390} with anger{H639} and wrath{H2534}, and your wrath{H639} came{H935}; and the time{H6256} to judge{H8199} the dead{H4191}, and to give{H5414} the wages{H7939} to your servants{H5650} the prophets{H5030}, and to the holy ones{H6918}, and to those who fear{H3372} your face{H6440}, to the small{H6996} and to the great{H1419}; and to destroy{H7843} those who destroyed{H7843} the earth{H776}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אַף וְחֵימָה ('anger and wrath,' H639+H2534) — a stock OT word-pair occurring as a formulaic doublet (Deut 29:27, Jer 21:5, 32:37, Ezek 5:15). Greek ὠργίσθησαν ('were angry') is a single verb. A back-translator from one Greek verb would produce a single Hebrew noun, not the OT's fixed two-word formula.

Uses מִפָּנֶיךָ ('your face/before you,' H6440) — 'those who fear your FACE/PRESENCE.' Greek has τὸ ὄνομά σου ('your NAME'). A back-translator from Greek 'your name' would write שִׁמְךָ (shimcha), not מִפָּנֶיךָ. The Hebrew expression ירא מפני ('fear from before') is a standard OT construction (Deut 28:10, Isa 41:5, Jer 5:22).

Uses הַשְׁחִית (H7843) for BOTH God's judgment and the destroyers' crime — the same root creating a measure-for-measure (מידה כנגד מידה) justice pattern: they 'destroyed' → God will 'destroy' them. The Hebrew reader hears the wordplay immediately.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'those who fear your FACE' (מפניך). Greek: 'those who fear your NAME' (τὸ ὄνομά σου). Different object of reverence.
Hebrew: 'anger and wrath' (two nouns). Greek: 'were angry' (one verb). Different expression.
translation_notes: אֵילּוּ (eilu — 'those') is a post-biblical Hebrew demonstrative pronoun, absent from the OT. Its appearance here marks the author as writing in later Hebrew, not translating from Greek.
'Wages' for שָׂכָר (sachar) — framing prophetic service as labor earning recompense (Gen 30:28, 31:8).

verses.translation: And the house{H1004} of prayer{H8605} of YHWH{H3068} was opened{H6605} in the heavens{H8064}, and the ark{H727} of the tablets{H3871} of the covenant{H1285} was seen{H7200} in his house{H1004} of prayer{H8605}; and there were voices{H6963} and thunders{H7482} and lightnings{H1300} and quakings{H7494} of the earth{H776}, and great{H1419} hail{H1259}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses אֲרוֹן לוּחוֹת הַבְּרִית ('the ark of the TABLETS of the covenant,' H727+H3871+H1285). Greek has ἡ κιβωτὸς τῆς διαθήκης αὐτοῦ ('the ark of his covenant'). The Hebrew adds לוּחוֹת ('tablets') — the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments stored inside the ark (Deut 9:9,11,15, 10:1-5, 1 Kings 8:9). A back-translator from Greek would write אֲרוֹן הַבְּרִית ('ark of the covenant') without adding 'tablets.' The Hebrew author knows what the ark CONTAINED.

Uses בֵּית תְּפִילָּה ('house of prayer,' H1004+H8605) TWICE — an echo of Isaiah 56:7 (כִּי בֵיתִי בֵּית תְּפִלָּה יִקָּרֵא לְכָל הָעַמִּים — 'for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples'). Greek has ναός ('temple/sanctuary'). A back-translator from Greek ναός would use הֵיכָל (heichal — 'temple') or מִקְדָּשׁ (miqdash — 'sanctuary'), NOT the Isaiah-specific phrase 'house of prayer.' This is the SAME term used in Rev 21:22.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'ark of the TABLETS of the covenant.' Greek: 'ark of his covenant.' Hebrew specifies the tablets.
Hebrew: 'house of prayer' (בית תפלה). Greek: 'temple' (ναός). Different term with different connotations.
translation_notes: 'House of prayer' — this is the phrase Yeshua himself used when cleansing the Temple (Matt 21:13, quoting Isaiah 56:7). The Hebrew author naturally uses Isaiah's own term.
textual_notes: The Sinai theophany parallel is unmistakable: voices, thunders, lightnings, and quaking (cf. Ex 19:16-18, 20:18). The opening of the heavenly house of prayer reveals the same covenant objects and phenomena that accompanied the original covenant.

verses.translation: And a great{H1419} sign{H5251} was seen{H7200} in the heavens{H8064}: a woman{H802} clothed{H3847} in the sun{H8121}, and the moon{H3394} under{H8478} her feet{H7272}, and upon her head{H7218} one crown{H3804} of twelve{H8147}{H6240} stars{H3556}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נֵס (nes, H5251 — 'sign/banner/standard') — the word for Moses' bronze serpent on a pole (Num 21:8-9) and for prophetic banners visible from afar (Isa 11:10, 13:2, 18:3, 49:22, 62:10). Greek has σημεῖον μέγα ('great sign'). A back-translator from Greek σημεῖον would use אוֹת (ot — 'sign'), the standard word for signs and wonders (Ex 4:8-9, Deut 4:34, Isa 7:14). The Hebrew נס carries connotations of a military standard RAISED HIGH for all to see — fundamentally different from אות.

Uses כֶּתֶר (keter, H3804 — 'royal crown/diadem') — the specific crown from Esther (1:11, 2:17, 6:8) and Proverbs (4:9, 12:4, 17:6). Greek has στέφανος ('victor's wreath/garland'). A back-translator from Greek στέφανος would use עֲטָרָה (atarah — 'wreath/garland,' H5850), which is the direct Hebrew equivalent of στέφανος. The Hebrew כתר is the ROYAL crown, not the athletic or victory wreath.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: נֵס ('sign/banner'). Greek: σημεῖον ('sign'). The Hebrew nuance of a raised standard is absent from Greek.
Hebrew: כֶּתֶר ('royal crown'). Greek: στέφανος ('victor's wreath'). Different type of crown.
translation_notes: אֶחָד used twice ('one woman,' 'one crown') — functioning as an indefinite article, a common later Hebrew usage.
textual_notes: The imagery of sun, moon, and twelve stars echoes Joseph's dream (Gen 37:9 — 'the sun and the moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me'). The woman wears Israel's patriarchal symbols.

verses.translation: And she was pregnant{H2030} and crying out{H6817}; and she was sitting{H3427} upon the birth-stool{H4866}, and she had much{H7235} anguish on account of the birthing{H3205}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הַמַּשְׁבֵּר (hamashber, H4866 — 'birth-stool/the breaking-place') — the specific term for the birthing seat where women sat during delivery (2 Kings 19:3 / Isa 37:3 — 'children have come to the mashber but there is no strength to bring forth'; Hos 13:13). Greek has βασανιζομένη τεκεῖν ('tormented to give birth'). The Hebrew gives the CONCRETE IMAGE of a woman on the birth-stool; the Greek gives an abstract description of torment. A back-translator from Greek would write מְעוּנָּה לָלֶדֶת ('tormented to deliver'), not invoke the birth-stool imagery.

Uses צוֹעֶקֶת (tso'eqet — 'crying out,' H6817) — the specific verb for crying out in distress under oppression. This is the EXODUS CRY VERB — Israel's cry under Egypt (Ex 2:23, Judg 3:9,15, 4:3, 6:7, 10:10). The woman's cry echoes Israel's cry in Egypt. Greek κράζουσα ('crying') is generic.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'sitting upon the birth-stool' (concrete physical image). Greek: 'tormented to give birth' (abstract description). Entirely different imagery.
Hebrew has a lacuna marked with brackets [ ] between the two clauses. The text may have originally contained additional material.
translation_notes: צַעַר (tsa'ar — 'anguish/pain') lacks a standard OT Strong's number; it is a post-biblical Hebrew form.
בִּשְׁבִיל (bishvil — 'on account of') is post-biblical Hebrew, absent from the OT. A back-translator working from Greek would use biblical מִפְּנֵי (mipnei) or בַּעֲבוּר (ba'avur).
textual_notes: 2 Kings 19:3 / Isaiah 37:3 — כִּי בָאוּ בָנִים עַד מַשְׁבֵּר וְכֹחַ אַיִן לְלֵדָה ('children have come to the birth-stool but there is no strength to deliver'). Hezekiah's crisis metaphor of a nation in labor. The same image applied to the woman of Revelation.

verses.translation: And another{H312} sign{H5251} was in the heavens{H8064}, and I saw{H7200} a dragon{H8577}; and it had seven{H7651} heads{H7218} and ten{H6235} horns{H7161}, and upon its heads{H7218} seven{H7651} crowns{H3804}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תַּנִּין (tannin, H8577 — 'dragon/sea-serpent') — the primordial chaos-creature of the OT: created by God (Gen 1:21), Egypt's serpent (Ex 7:9-12), the chaos-monster slain by YHWH (Isa 27:1 — 'Leviathan the fleeing serpent, the tannin in the sea'; Isa 51:9 — 'was it not you who cut Rahab, who pierced the tannin?'), and Pharaoh himself (Ezek 29:3, 32:2). Greek δράκων ('dragon') is generic. The Hebrew word carries an entire OT mythology of YHWH's primordial victory over chaos.

Uses כְּתָרִים (ketarim — 'royal crowns,' H3804) — the same royal crown word as verse 6. Greek has διαδήματα ('diadems'). While both indicate royalty, the Hebrew keter specifically links the dragon's false kingship to the Esther/Proverbs crown vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Greek adds πυρρός ('fiery red') to describe the dragon — absent from Hebrew. The Hebrew dragon has no color.
Greek calls it μέγας δράκων ('great dragon'). The Hebrew does not say 'great' here (it reserves גדול for the sign, not the dragon itself).
translation_notes: The tannin is consistently associated with the sea and with Egypt in the OT. Identifying it here sets up the Exodus typology that runs through the chapter — the dragon/Pharaoh pursuing the woman/Israel.
textual_notes: Isaiah 27:1 — 'In that day YHWH with his hard and great and strong sword will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he will slay the TANNIN that is in the sea.' The eschatological defeat of the tannin is an Isaiah prophecy being fulfilled.

verses.translation: And its tail{H2180} took{H3947} a third{H7992} of the stars{H3556} and cast{H2236} them upon the earth{H776}. And the dragon{H8577} tread{H1869} before{H6440} the woman{H802} who was to give birth{H3205}, in order to devour{H398} the child{H3206} when it was born{H3205}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses דָּרַךְ (darach, H1869 — 'to tread/march') — the verb for treading grapes in a winepress (Isa 63:3, Lam 1:15), bending the war bow (Ps 7:13, 11:2, 37:14), and military advance (Num 24:17, Judg 5:21). Greek ἕστηκεν means simply 'stood.' A back-translator from Greek would use עָמַד (amad — 'stood,' H5975). The Hebrew verb implies aggressive, predatory ADVANCE — the dragon MARCHES toward the woman, not merely stands before her.

Uses זָרַק (zaraq, H2236 — 'cast/hurled/threw') — a verb whose primary OT context is the priestly sprinkling/casting of blood on the altar (Lev 1:5,11, 3:2,8,13, 7:2). Greek βάλλω ('throw/cast') is generic. A back-translator would use הִשְׁלִיךְ (hishlich — 'cast/threw,' H7993), the common throwing verb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'tread before' (דרך — aggressive march). Greek: 'stood before' (ἕστηκεν — stationary). Fundamentally different postures.
Hebrew: בְּאִם שֶׁנּוֹלָד ('when/if it was born') — using the conditional particle אם. Greek: ὅταν τέκῃ ('whenever she gives birth') — temporal conjunction. The Hebrew carries a shade of uncertainty.
translation_notes: 'Tread' for דרך preserves the Hebrew verb's aggressive, military-advance connotation — this is not a dragon waiting but a dragon advancing.
textual_notes: Daniel 8:10 — 'It grew great, even to the host of heaven. And some of the host and some of the stars it cast down to the ground.' The dragon's tail sweeping stars echoes Daniel's vision of the horn casting down the heavenly host.

verses.translation: And she gave birth{H3205} to one son{H1121}, the one who leads{H5090} the peoples{H5971} with a rod{H7626} of iron{H1270}; and the child{H3206} was brought{H935} before{H6440} YHWH{H3068} and his throne{H3678}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הַמְנַהֵג (hamnaheg — 'the one who leads/drives,' from H5090 נהג) — the verb for leading flocks (Gen 31:18, Ex 3:1), driving chariots (2 Kings 9:20), and guiding nations (Isa 11:6). Greek μέλλει ποιμαίνειν means 'is about to SHEPHERD.' A back-translator from Greek ποιμαίνω would use רוֹעֶה (ro'eh — 'shepherding,' H7462), NOT מנהג. The Hebrew uses a leading/driving verb; the Greek uses a shepherding verb.

Uses מוּבָא (muva — 'was brought,' passive of H935 בוא) — implying reverent PRESENTATION before the throne. Greek ἡρπάσθη means 'was SNATCHED UP/seized' (from ἁρπάζω). These are radically different: Hebrew describes liturgical presentation; Greek describes urgent rescue. A back-translator from Greek would use נֶחְטַף (nechtaf — 'was snatched').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the one who LEADS' (present participle — ongoing quality). Greek: 'who is ABOUT TO shepherd' (μέλλει — future/imminent). Different temporal aspect and different verb.
Hebrew: 'was brought before YHWH' (reverent presentation). Greek: 'was caught up to God' (ἡρπάσθη — urgent rescue). Different action and different divine name.
Hebrew: 'the peoples' (העמים). Greek: 'all the nations' (πάντα τὰ ἔθνη). Greek adds 'all.'
translation_notes: שֵׁבֶט (shevet, H7626) means both 'rod/staff' and 'tribe' in Hebrew. The Psalm 2:9 allusion (תְּרֹעֵם בְּשֵׁבֶט בַּרְזֶל — 'you shall break them with a rod of iron') is clear in both Hebrew and Greek traditions.
textual_notes: Psalm 2:9 — the messianic psalm of the son who inherits the nations. Both Hebrew and Greek Revelation quote it, but the Hebrew uses the original Hebrew of the psalm.

verses.translation: And the woman{H802} went{H1980} into the wilderness{H4057}, since there was prepared{H3559} for her there a place{H4725} from YHWH{H3068}, to sustain her there a thousand{H505} and two{H8147} hundred{H3967} and sixty{H8346} days{H3117}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הָלְכָה (halchah — 'she went,' H1980) — neutral movement. Greek ἔφυγεν means 'she FLED' (from φεύγω). A back-translator from Greek would use בָּרְחָה (barchah — 'she fled,' H1272). The Hebrew says she WENT; the Greek says she FLED. The Hebrew presents a purposeful journey; the Greek presents an escape.

Uses כֵּיוָן שׁ (keivan she — 'since/because') — a post-biblical Hebrew conjunction ABSENT from the OT entirely. Greek has ὅπου ('where' — locative). The Hebrew constructs a CAUSAL clause ('since there was prepared'); the Greek constructs a LOCATIVE clause ('where she has a place'). A back-translator from Greek 'where' would write אֲשֶׁר שָׁם or בַּמָּקוֹם שׁ ('in the place where'), not the causal כיון ש.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'she went' (הלכה — purposeful journey). Greek: 'she fled' (ἔφυγεν — escape). Different posture.
Hebrew: 'since there was prepared for her a place from YHWH' (causal clause naming YHWH). Greek: 'where she has a place prepared by God' (locative clause naming 'God').
Hebrew: 'to sustain her' (one actor implied — YHWH). Greek: 'that they may nourish her' (τρέφωσιν — third person plural, unspecified agents).
translation_notes: לְפַרְנֵס (lefarnes — 'to sustain/provide for') is a post-biblical Hebrew/Aramaic verb extensively used in Rabbinic literature. No OT Strong's number. A back-translator from Greek τρέφω would use כִּלְכֵּל (kilkel — 'to sustain,' Gen 45:11, 47:12) or זוּן (zun — 'to feed'). The natural use of פרנס marks a Hebrew author writing in contemporary vocabulary.
textual_notes: The Exodus typology: the woman goes to the wilderness (מדבר) where YHWH sustains her — exactly as Israel went into the wilderness where YHWH sustained them with manna (Ex 16). The 1,260 days = 3.5 years, half of 7.

verses.translation: And war{H4421} was made{H6213} in the heavens{H8064}: the messenger{H4397} Mikhael{H4317} with his messengers{H4397} fought{H3898} against the dragon{H8577}, and its messengers{H4397} fought{H3898} against them.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נַעֲשָׂה מִלְחָמָה ('war was made,' from עשה H6213 + מלחמה H4421) — the OT military formula for conducting war (Josh 11:18, Judg 3:10, 1 Sam 28:15, 2 Sam 11:7). Greek ἐγένετο πόλεμος ('war arose/happened,' from γίνομαι). A back-translator from γίνομαι would use הָיָה (hayah — 'was'), not the active formula נעשה ('was made').

The Hebrew makes the war explicitly BILATERAL: 'Mikhael with his messengers fought... and its messengers fought against them' (ומלאכיו לחמו עימם). Both sides actively engage. Greek is more compressed.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the messenger Mikhael' (המלאך מיכאל — singular title, then with his messengers). Greek: 'Michael and his angels' (Μιχαὴλ καὶ οἱ ἄγγελοι αὐτοῦ). Minor structural difference — Hebrew emphasizes Mikhael's role as THE messenger.
translation_notes: מִיכָאֵל (Mikhael, H4317) — meaning 'Who is like El?' — the only named archangel in the OT (Dan 10:13,21, 12:1). His name is itself a theological question.
textual_notes: Daniel 12:1 — 'At that time shall arise Mikhael, the great prince who stands over the sons of your people.' The Hebrew Revelation fulfills Daniel's prophecy of Mikhael's eschatological war.

verses.translation: And they did not prevail{H5329}, and also{H1571} their place{H4725} was not found{H4672} anymore{H5750} in the heavens{H8064}.

greek_deviations: Very close correspondence between Hebrew and Greek here. Both say the dragon's forces did not prevail and their place was no longer found in heaven.
translation_notes: נִצְּחוּ (nitschu — from H5329 נצח) — the same root as 'eternity/enduring' (נֶצַח). The verb implies lasting, decisive victory — or here, the lack of it.

verses.translation: And the great{H1419} dragon{H8577} was cast{H7993} outside{H2351}, the one called{H7121} the Adversary{H7854}, the destroyer{H7843} and the one who incites{H5496} all{H3605} the world{H5769}; and he with his messengers{H4397} were cast{H7993} upon the earth{H776} to dwell{H1752} there.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew has TWO functional titles — הַמַּשְׁחִית ('the destroyer,' from H7843 שחת) AND הַמַּסִּית ('the inciter/seducer,' from H5496 סות). Greek has only ὁ πλανῶν ('the one deceiving') — one function. Moreover, מַסִּית (masit) is the specific TORAH LEGAL TERM for one who incites others to idolatry (Deut 13:7[6]) — a capital crime. A back-translator from Greek πλανάω would use מַתְעֶה (mat'eh — 'deceiver'), not the Deuteronomy 13 legal terminology.

CRITICAL: Greek adds ὁ ὄφις ὁ ἀρχαῖος ('the ancient serpent') — a title ENTIRELY ABSENT from the Hebrew. The Hebrew does NOT connect the dragon to the Genesis serpent (נחש). Greek also adds Διάβολος ('Devil') — absent from Hebrew. The Hebrew has one title (שטן — Adversary) plus two functions (destroyer, inciter); the Greek has four titles (serpent, devil, dragon, Satan) plus one function (deceiver). These are fundamentally different naming schemes.

Uses לָדוּר שָׁם ('to dwell there') — a clause ABSENT from Greek, which simply says ἐβλήθη εἰς τὴν γῆν ('was cast to the earth'). The Hebrew adds PURPOSE — the casting is a sentence of EXILE, not mere removal. The dragon is sentenced to dwell on earth.
greek_deviations: Greek adds 'the ancient serpent' (ὁ ὄφις ὁ ἀρχαῖος) and 'the Devil' (Διάβολος) — both absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'the destroyer and the inciter' (two functional titles). Greek: 'the deceiver' (one function).
Hebrew: 'all the world' (כל העולם — olam, 'world/age'). Greek: 'the whole inhabited earth' (τὴν οἰκουμένην ὅλην — oikoumene).
Hebrew adds 'to dwell there' (לדור שם) — absent from Greek.
translation_notes: שָׂטָן (satan, H7854) means 'adversary/accuser/opposer' (Job 1-2, Zech 3:1, 1 Chr 21:1). The Greek Σατανᾶς is a transliteration of the Hebrew — the Greek BORROWED the Hebrew term. Hebrew is the source language for this title.
textual_notes: The verb שחת (H7843 — 'destroy') connects this verse to verse 4 where the same root appears twice: 'to destroy those who destroyed the earth.' The dragon IS the destroyer — this title links him to the destroyers of v4.

verses.translation: And I heard{H8085} a great{H1419} voice{H6963} in the heavens{H8064} which said{H559}: Now is seen{H7200} the might{H1369} of our Elohim{H430} and his anointed{H4899}, since he was cast{H7993} outside{H2351} — this one who was at all{H3605} times{H6256} an adversary{H7854} against them.

one_way_hebrew: Uses גְּבוּרוֹת (gevurot — 'mighty deeds/power,' H1369 plural) — a specifically Hebrew concept of God's power-acts (Deut 3:24, Ps 20:6, 71:16, 106:2, 145:4,12, 150:2). Greek has THREE separate nouns: σωτηρία ('salvation'), δύναμις ('power'), and βασιλεία ('kingdom'). A back-translator from three Greek nouns would not collapse them into the single Hebrew gevurot. The Hebrew carries a richer concept — all God's mighty acts — in one word.

Uses עַכְשָׁיו (achshav — 'now') — a post-biblical Hebrew word absent from the OT (biblical Hebrew uses עַתָּה — attah). A Hebrew author writing naturally uses achshav; a back-translator working from Greek ἄρτι would choose the biblical עתה.

Uses כָּל עֵת ('at all times') for the adversary's activity. Greek has ἡμέρας καὶ νυκτός ('day and night'). A back-translator from Greek would write יוֹמָם וָלַיְלָה ('day and night'), not the abstract כל עת.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the might of our Elohim and his anointed' (one attribute shared by two). Greek: 'the salvation, and power, and kingdom of our God, AND the authority of his Christ' (four attributes split across two). Massively expanded in Greek.
Hebrew: 'now is SEEN' (נתראה — made visible). Greek: 'now has COME' (ἄρτι ἐγένετο — came about). Different — visibility vs. arrival.

Hebrew: 'at all times an adversary against them.' Greek: 'who accused them before our God day and night.' Greek specifies the venue ('before God'), the time pattern ('day and night'), and the action ('accused'). Hebrew is more concise.
translation_notes: Hebrew uses the verbal noun לשטן (lesatan — 'as adversary') rather than the title השטן ('the Adversary'). He functioned as an adversary; it was his role.

verses.translation: And they overcame{H5329} him by the hand{H3027} of the blood{H1818} of the lamb{H7716}, and by the hand{H3027} of the word{H1697} of their testimony{H5715}; and they reckoned{H2803} their lives{H2416} as nothing.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עַל יַד ('by the hand of,' H5921+H3027) — a standard Hebrew idiom meaning 'by means of / through the agency of' (2 Sam 14:30, 2 Kings 14:27). Literally 'upon the hand of.' Greek uses the simple preposition διά ('through'). A Hebrew author naturally reaches for this concrete body-part idiom; a back-translator from Greek would use the preposition בְּ (be — 'by/through').

CRITICAL: Uses וְחִשְּׁבוּ אֶת חַיֵּיהֶם לִכְלוּם ('and they RECKONED their lives as NOTHING,' from H2803 חשב — 'to reckon/account'). Greek has οὐκ ἠγάπησαν τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτῶν ἄχρι θανάτου ('they did NOT LOVE their SOULS unto DEATH'). These are ENTIRELY different expressions — one about valuation (reckoning as nothing), the other about affection (not loving unto death). A back-translator from Greek would write לֹא אָהֲבוּ אֶת נַפְשׁוֹתָם עַד מָוֶת ('they did not love their souls unto death'). The Hebrew concept is economic — they assessed the VALUE of their lives at zero.

Uses שֶׂה (seh, H7716) — the Passover lamb of Exodus 12:3-5, consistent with its use throughout this Hebrew Revelation (cf. Rev 21:9). Greek ἀρνίον ('little lamb') is a diminutive form that does not carry the Passover specificity.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'they reckoned their lives as nothing.' Greek: 'they did not love their lives unto death.' Completely different expression — valuation vs. affection.
Hebrew: חַיֵּיהֶם ('their lives,' H2416 — the state of being alive). Greek: τὴν ψυχήν ('their soul/life,' ψυχή). Different word — concrete 'lives' vs. 'soul.'
translation_notes: כְּלוּם (klum — 'nothing') is a post-biblical Hebrew word, absent from the OT. Common in Rabbinic literature. No standard Strong's number.

verses.translation: And because of this, rejoice{H8055}, O heavens{H8064}, and all{H3605} who are in them! And woe{H188} to those who dwell upon the earth{H776} and upon the sea{H3220}, for the Adversary{H7854} has come down{H3381} to you in great{H1419} burning{H2740} anger{H639}, knowing{H3045} that he has but a small{H4592} season{H2165}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חֲרוֹן אַף ('burning anger/fierce wrath,' H2740+H639) — a fixed OT compound expression occurring 39 times (Ex 32:12, Num 25:4, 32:14, Deut 13:17, Josh 7:26, Judg 2:14, 2 Kings 23:26, etc.). This is formulaic Hebrew — a set phrase that a native speaker reproduces automatically. Greek θυμὸν μέγαν ('great wrath') is generic. A back-translator from Greek would write חֵמָה גְּדוֹלָה ('great wrath') or כַּעַס גָּדוֹל ('great anger'), NOT the fixed OT formula חרון אף.

Uses זְמָן (zman, H2165 — 'time/season') — an Aramaic-influenced word rare in the OT (only Neh 2:6, Esth 9:27,31, Eccl 3:1, Dan 2:16,21). This is NOT the standard biblical Hebrew עֵת (et — 'time'). A back-translator from Greek καιρός would choose the standard biblical עת, not the Aramaic-tinged זמן. Its use marks a Hebrew author writing in later Hebrew.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'burning anger' (חרון אף — stock OT compound). Greek: 'great wrath' (θυμὸν μέγαν). Different expression.
Hebrew: 'because of this' (ובשביל זה — post-biblical). Greek: 'therefore' (διὰ τοῦτο).
translation_notes: בִּשְׁבִיל (bishvil — 'because of') and הַדָּרִים (hadarim — 'those who dwell') are both post-biblical Hebrew forms. A back-translator would not produce these.
אֵילּוּ (eilu — 'those') appears again — the same post-biblical demonstrative as in verse 4.

verses.translation: And when the dragon{H8577} saw{H7200} that it was cast{H7993} upon the earth{H776}, it pursued{H7291} the woman{H802} who had given birth{H3205}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses רָדַף (radaf, H7291 — 'to pursue/chase/persecute') — a word saturated with Exodus resonance: the Egyptians PURSUING Israel (Ex 14:4,8,9,23, 15:9), Laban pursuing Jacob (Gen 31:23,36), enemies pursuing the righteous (Deut 28:22,45, Lev 26:17,36). The dragon/tannin PURSUING the woman through the wilderness replays the Exodus — Pharaoh pursuing Israel. Greek ἐδίωξεν ('pursued/persecuted') corresponds, but lacks the Exodus-specific weight.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the woman who had given birth' (שילדה — without specifying what). Greek: 'the woman who had given birth to the MALE CHILD' (τὴν γυναῖκα ἥτις ἔτεκεν τὸν ἄρρενα). Greek specifies; Hebrew is concise.
translation_notes: כֵּיוָן שׁ (keivan she — 'when/since') appears for the third time in this chapter (vv. 11, 15a, 17) — a consistent post-biblical Hebrew conjunction throughout.
textual_notes: The Exodus pattern is now explicit: the tannin (= Pharaoh, Ezek 29:3) pursues (רדף — the Exodus verb) the woman (= Israel) into the wilderness (מדבר) where YHWH sustains her. Every element has a Torah parallel.

verses.translation: And two{H8147} wings{H3671} were given{H5414} to the woman{H802}, like a great{H1419} eagle{H5404}, in order to go{H1980} into the wilderness{H4057}, to the place{H4725} which YHWH{H3068} gave{H5414} her, to sustain her there a time{H6256} and two{H8147} times{H6256} and a half{H2677}, from before{H6440} the dragon{H8577}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses כְּנֶשֶׁר גָּדוֹל ('like a great eagle,' H5404) — directly echoing Exodus 19:4: 'You have seen what I did to Egypt, and I bore you on EAGLES' WINGS (כַּנְפֵי נְשָׁרִים) and brought you to myself.' And Deuteronomy 32:11: 'As an EAGLE (נשר) stirs up its nest, hovers over its young, spreads its WINGS (כנפיו), takes them, bears them on its pinions.' The woman-Israel receives eagle wings for wilderness flight — EXACTLY the Exodus imagery. Greek τοῦ ἀετοῦ τοῦ μεγάλου ('the great eagle') corresponds, but the Hebrew naturally integrates with the Torah's eagle-wing theology.

Uses לֵילֵךְ ('to GO,' H1980) — even though the woman has wings, she GOES (walks) into the wilderness. Greek ἵνα πέτηται means 'that she might FLY' (from πέτομαι). A back-translator from 'fly' would use לָעוּף (la'uf — 'to fly'). The Hebrew uses ordinary travel language — like Israel GOING through the wilderness on foot, even under divine wings.

Uses עֵת... עִיתִּים (et... ittim — 'a time... times') — echoing Daniel 7:25, 12:7 in the Hebrew original. The plural עיתים is natural Hebrew for the plural of עת. Greek καιρὸν καὶ καιρούς also echoes Daniel's LXX. Both traditions quote Daniel, but the Hebrew preserves the original Hebrew form.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'to GO' (הלך) into the wilderness. Greek: 'to FLY' (πέτομαι). Different — walking vs. flying.
Hebrew: 'to the place which YHWH gave her' (naming YHWH as source). Greek: 'to her place' (no divine attribution).
Hebrew: לפרנס ('to sustain') — same post-biblical verb as v11. Greek: τρέφεται ('she is nourished').
textual_notes: Exodus 19:4 — וָאֶשָּׂא אֶתְכֶם עַל כַּנְפֵי נְשָׁרִים וָאָבִא אֶתְכֶם אֵלָי ('I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself'). The woman's eagle wings are a deliberate replay of the Exodus deliverance.
Daniel 7:25 / 12:7 — 'a time, times, and half a time.' The same duration as the 1,260 days of v11 (3.5 years), connecting both wilderness periods.

verses.translation: And the dragon{H8577} cast{H7993} after{H310} the woman{H802} waters{H4325} [from its mouth{H6310}] like a great{H1419} sea{H3220}, in order to silence{H8252} her.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses כְּיָם גָּדוֹל ('like a great SEA,' H3220). Greek has ὕδωρ ὡς ποταμόν ('water like a RIVER'). The Hebrew compares the flood to a SEA (יָם) — the cosmological chaos-waters, the sea YHWH split at the Exodus (Ex 14), the sea where the tannin dwells (Isa 27:1). A back-translator from Greek ποταμός ('river') would use נָהָר (nahar — 'river,' H5104), NOT ים. The tannin/sea-serpent attacking with sea-waters is a coherent mythological image in Hebrew; 'river' breaks the connection.

Uses לְהַשְׁקִיט (lehashqit — 'to silence/make still,' from H8252 שקט). Greek has ποταμοφόρητον ποιήσῃ ('to make her flood-carried'). The Hebrew euphemistically describes drowning as 'silencing' or 'making still' — the woman would be made quiet (dead). A back-translator from Greek would use לִשְׁטוֹף (lishtof — 'to flood/wash away'), not the 'silencing' verb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'like a great SEA.' Greek: 'like a RIVER.' Sea vs. river — fundamentally different cosmological imagery.
Hebrew: 'to silence her' (euphemism for destroy). Greek: 'to make her flood-carried' (mechanism of destruction).
[מפיו] ('from its mouth') appears in brackets in the Hebrew text, suggesting textual uncertainty or editorial restoration. Greek has ἐκ τοῦ στόματος αὐτοῦ ('from his mouth') without ambiguity.
translation_notes: Brackets around [מפיו] preserved from the source text, indicating this phrase may be a later restoration or is textually uncertain.
textual_notes: The tannin/sea-serpent casting SEA-waters against the woman continues the Exodus cosmic-battle imagery: YHWH defeated the tannin and the sea at the Exodus (Isa 51:9-10 — 'Was it not you who cut Rahab, who pierced the tannin? Was it not you who dried up the sea?'). Now the tannin retaliates with the sea.

verses.translation: But the woman{H802} had deliverance{H3444} from the ground{H127}, for it opened{H6605} its mouth{H6310} and swallowed{H1104} the waters{H4325} which the dragon{H8577} had cast{H7993} after her.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses אֲדָמָה (adamah, H127 — 'ground/soil') where Greek has γῆ (ge — 'earth'). This is the SAME distinction noted in Rev 21:1. A back-translator from Greek γῆ would use אֶרֶץ (erets — 'earth'), not אדמה. The use of adamah here DIRECTLY echoes Numbers 16:30-33 where the ADAMAH opened its mouth and swallowed Korah: וּפָצְתָה הָאֲדָמָה אֶת פִּיהָ וּבָלְעָה אֹתָם ('and the GROUND opened its mouth and swallowed them'). The verbal parallel is unmistakable.

CRITICAL: The phrase פָּתְחָה אֶת פִּיהָ וּבָלַע ('opened its mouth and swallowed') nearly quotes Numbers 16:32 verbatim: וַתִּפְתַּח הָאָרֶץ אֶת פִּיהָ וַתִּבְלַע אֹתָם ('and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them'). The Hebrew Revelation deliberately echoes the Korah rebellion narrative — the same ground that swallowed YHWH's enemies now swallows the dragon's weapon. A back-translator from Greek would reproduce this pattern only by coincidence.

Uses יְשׁוּעָה (yeshu'ah, H3444 — 'salvation/deliverance') — the grand OT word for divine rescue (Ex 14:13, 15:2, Judg 15:18, 1 Sam 11:13, Ps 3:8). Greek ἐβοήθησεν means merely 'helped' (from βοηθέω). A back-translator from Greek 'helped' would use עָזַר (azar — 'helped,' H5826), not the theologically loaded ישועה. The Hebrew frames this as a divine DELIVERANCE act.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the woman had DELIVERANCE from the ground' (ישועה — grand salvation). Greek: 'the earth HELPED the woman' (ἐβοήθησεν — simply helped). Different scale of imagery.
Hebrew: 'the GROUND' (אדמה, H127). Greek: 'the earth' (γῆ). Different Hebrew term, carrying the Numbers 16 resonance.
translation_notes: 'Ground' for adamah (not 'earth') preserves the critical distinction from erets and the Numbers 16 allusion — the adamah that swallowed Korah now swallows the dragon's flood.
textual_notes: Numbers 16:30-33 — The ground (אדמה) opening its mouth (פצתה את פיה) and swallowing (ובלעה) Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. In Numbers, the ground swallows rebels; in Revelation, the ground swallows the dragon's weapon to SAVE the woman. Same mechanism, inverted purpose — judgment becomes salvation.

verses.translation: And the dragon{H8577} was filled{H4390} with anger{H639} on account of the woman{H802}, and went{H1980} to wage war{H3898} with the remnant{H3498} of her seed{H2233}, those who keep{H6213} the commandments{H4687} of YHWH{H3068} and who believe{H539} in the testimony{H5715} of his anointed{H4899}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הַנּוֹתָרִים (hanotarim — 'the remnant/survivors,' from H3498 יתר) — carrying the weight of Isaiah's remnant theology (Isa 1:9, 10:20-22, 11:11,16, 37:4,31-32, Mic 5:7[6]). Greek τῶν λοιπῶν ('the rest/remaining') is neutral. The Hebrew 'remnant of her seed' echoes Isaiah's 'remnant of Israel.' This is a theologically loaded term in Hebrew; a flat word in Greek.

Uses הָעוֹשִׂים ('those who DO/KEEP,' from H6213 עשה) the commandments — the TORAH'S OWN VERB for observing commandments (Ex 20:6 — עוֹשֵׂי מִצְוֹתָי 'those who do my commandments'; Deut 5:10, 6:25, 7:11, 26:16). Greek τηρούντων ('keeping/guarding') uses τηρέω. A back-translator from Greek would use שׁוֹמְרִים (shomrim — 'keeping/guarding,' from שמר H8104), the natural Hebrew equivalent of τηρέω. But the Hebrew author uses עשה — the Torah's specific verb.

Uses עֵדוּת שֶׁל מְשִׁיחוֹ ('testimony of his ANOINTED,' H5715+H4899) — no personal name, only the messianic TITLE. Greek has μαρτυρίαν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ('the testimony of Jesus Christ') — with the personal name. A back-translator from Greek would transliterate ישוע or use both name and title. The Hebrew uses only the generic title משיחו ('his anointed'), which any Jewish reader would understand as the expected messianic figure.

Uses מִצְוֹת יַהְוֶה ('commandments of YHWH,' H4687+H3068) — a standard Torah expression (Deut 8:6, 11:1, 26:17, 28:9, 30:16). Greek has τὰς ἐντολὰς τοῦ θεοῦ ('the commandments of God'). The Hebrew uses the personal Name; the Greek uses the generic 'God.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'testimony of his anointed' (משיחו — title only, no personal name). Greek: 'testimony of Jesus Christ' (named).
Hebrew: 'those who DO the commandments of YHWH' (עושים — Torah verb, YHWH — personal Name). Greek: 'those who KEEP the commandments of God' (τηρούντων — different verb, θεοῦ — generic).
Hebrew: נתמלא באף ('was filled with anger'). Greek: ὠργίσθη ('was wroth'). Hebrew is more vivid — filled to capacity with anger.
translation_notes: עֵדוּת (edut, H5715 — 'testimony') is the specific word for the covenant tablets stored in the ark (Ex 25:16,21, 31:18, 32:15, 40:20 — לוּחוֹת הָעֵדוּת 'the tablets of the testimony'). This creates a link back to verse 5 where the ark of the TABLETS of the covenant was seen.
textual_notes: The chapter ends by defining the remnant with TWO markers: (1) keeping YHWH's commandments (Torah observance) and (2) believing in the testimony of his anointed (messianic faith). The Hebrew presents these as complementary, not competing.

chapter_notes.summary: Revelation 12 in the Hebrew (spanning Greek 11:15–12:17) is structured as a sustained Exodus replay. The vocabulary is drawn from Torah and Prophets with remarkable specificity: נס (sign/banner, not the standard אות), תנין (the primordial chaos sea-serpent of Isaiah 27:1 and Ezekiel 29:3), משבר (birth-stool from 2 Kings 19:3), חרון אף (the fixed OT burning-anger formula), eagle wings (Exodus 19:4, Deuteronomy 32:11), and the adamah that opens its mouth and swallows (Numbers 16:30-33). The chapter contains at least 20 clear one-way translation markers — cases where the Hebrew could not plausibly derive from the Greek: (1) ארון לוחות הברית ('ark of the TABLETS of the covenant') vs. Greek's bare 'ark of the covenant'; (2) בית תפלה ('house of prayer,' Isaiah 56:7) vs. Greek 'temple'; (3) the tripartite divine-name play ההיה והוה ויהיה unpacking YHWH into was/is/shall-be — impossible to generate from the Greek ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν; (4) אדמה ('ground') echoing Numbers 16 vs. Greek generic γῆ; (5) ישועה ('deliverance') vs. Greek 'helped'; (6) כים גדול ('like a great SEA') vs. Greek 'like a river'; (7) the dragon TREADS (דרך) toward the woman vs. Greek 'stood'; (8) two titles — המשחית ('the destroyer') and המסית (the Deuteronomy 13 idolatry-incitement term) — vs. Greek's single 'deceiver'; (9) 'they reckoned their lives as nothing' vs. Greek 'they did not love their lives unto death'; (10) מעולם ועד עולם (the psalm formula) vs. Greek 'unto the ages of ages'; (11) ימשל ('shall rule,' governance) vs. Greek βασιλεύσει ('shall reign as king'); (12) YHWH throughout vs. Greek 'God'; (13) משיחו ('his anointed') vs. Greek 'Jesus Christ'; (14) Hebrew omits 'ancient serpent' which Greek adds; (15) Hebrew adds לדור שם ('to dwell there') absent from Greek; (16) מובא ('was brought,' reverent presentation) vs. Greek ἡρπάσθη ('was snatched up,' urgent rescue); (17) מפניך ('your face') vs. Greek 'your name'; (18) להשקיט ('to silence') vs. Greek 'to sweep away by flood'; (19) מתפללים ('praying') vs. Greek 'worshipping'; (20) העשירים ('the rich') vs. Greek 'the kingdoms.' The chapter also features consistent post-biblical Hebrew forms (פרנס, עכשיו, כיון ש, זמן, בשביל, כלום, אילו) that a back-translator would never produce. The Exodus typology runs through every section: the tannin/Pharaoh pursues the woman/Israel with sea-waters into the wilderness where YHWH sustains her on eagle's wings, and the adamah that once swallowed Korah now swallows the enemy's weapon to deliver her.
